chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Jameel, and Muhammad ibn Humran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the free man upon whom fasting of two consecutive months is obligatory due to Dhikr (Zihar), so he fasts one month then falls sick. He said: He starts again, and if he increased upon the other month by a day or two days, he builds upon what remains.

key_terms.بَنَى عَلَى مَا بَقِيَ: He builds upon what remains (continuing the count without full restart)
key_terms.صَوْمُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ: Fasting of two consecutive months, a specific expiation (kaffarah)
key_terms.ظِهَارٍ: Zihar, a pre-Islamic form of divorce where a husband declares his wife like his mother's back, requiring expiation
key_terms.يَسْتَقْبِلُ: He starts again (referring to restarting the count or continuing)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for expiation fasting if interrupted by illness for a few days?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of *al-bina'* (building upon) in the expiation of *Zihar*, demonstrating the Shia juristic view that minor interruptions due to valid excuses like illness do not invalidate the consecutiveness (*tatabbu*) of the fast. It highlights the flexibility within the obligation, allowing the individual to resume from where they left off rather than restarting the two-month period, provided the break is brief.
